newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO-Russia dialogue to move up a gear.
newsitem.headline: NATO-Russia dialogue to move up a gear.

text.p: NATO and Russia step up the pace of their diplomacy this week on a future relationship which would allow the alliance to expand into former communist Europe without creating a major crisis in European security.

NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, the man charged by the alliance with negotiating a new, all-embracing post-Cold War deal with Moscow, returns to Moscow next weekend for more talks with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.
The two men will for the first time have drafts of a possible future agreement on a NATO-Russia Council, a new forum allowing permanent and across-the-board consultations on security issues.
"There will be many brackets and so on, but they will have working documents," said one alliance official, adding Solana's team would be in Moscow from Tuesday to work on the proposals.
Moscow wants any documents between the two to be legally binding and to contain commitments that NATO's military infrastructure will not be moved eastwards.

NATO favours a more flexible approach. It says the new deal, endorsed by alliance heads of state, will be politically binding, but a treaty would be unwieldy and take months to pass through national legislatures.

It also says it has no plans to move military hardware eastwards, but says it cannot tie its hands in advance by pledging in effect never to do so and certain minimum works, such as upgrading communications and airfields, must be done.
"NATO may be becoming a political organisation, but it is also remaining a military one," said one official. "We have to be able to honour (military) commitments to new members."
The impassive Primakov -- a former spy-master -- was in London last week, once again stressing Moscow's opposition to alliance enlargement.

But behind the rhetoric, diplomats say Moscow has clearly decided to try to clinch some sort of deal ahead of a NATO summit in July in Madrid at which the alliance will invite some former Warsaw Pact countries to join.

President Boris Yeltsin has said quite openly his country's tactics are to stall the process for as long as possible but that he expected to see some form of compromise when he meets President Bill Clinton in Helsinki on March 20-21.

Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic lead the field of a dozen countries clamouring to join the most powerful military alliance ever-assembled with Slovenia and Romania making late last-minute pushes for inclusion in the first round.

With the West now falling over itself to win Moscow's approval, diplomats say Russia realises it has a chance to strike a deal now and then focus its attention on extending an expected two-year negotiation and ratification process.
"By entering into real dialogue now, the Russians hope the whole thing will irrelevent by the time it actually happens," said one alliance diplomat.

The package on offer for the Russians includes an overhaul of the Conventional Forces in Europe treaty to take on board many of Moscow's concerns by setting ceilings on the number of troops allowed in any one area, regardless of nationality.

Separately, the United States is prepared to offer cuts in its armoury of sea-based nuclear missiles if Moscow proceeds with plans to dismantle many of its more sophisticated and deadly land-based systems.
